record.paper_title: The Status of Polycyclic Group-Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: Determine whether cryptosystems based on polycyclic groups, especially those using infinite polycyclic groups, are resistant to cryptanalysis by quantum algorithms. Equivalently, establish whether such polycyclic group-based cryptosystems remain secure against quantum computers, in light of the source text's observation that known quantum algorithms discussed there apply to finite-group settings rather than infinite groups.

evidence.quote: Of particular interest is to show that cryptosystems using infinite polycyclic groups are resistant to cryptanalysis on a quantum com- puter.
Despite these developments in the use quantum algorithms for finite groups, there are no known quantum algorithms that are applicable to infinite groups.
(10) Are polycyclic group-based cryptosystems resistant to quantum algorithms?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A group G is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series G = G_0 ⊵ G_1 ⊵ ⋯ ⊵ G_n = {1} in which each successive quotient G_i/G_{i+1} is cyclic. Polycyclic groups are finitely presented, and their word, conjugacy, and isomorphism problems are decidable; infinite polycyclic groups (for example, those arising as fundamental groups of certain solvmanifolds, or as the rational points of unipotent or solvable arithmetic groups) form a well-studied class generalizing finitely generated nilpotent groups.

Numerous public-key cryptographic schemes have been proposed whose security rests on computational problems in polycyclic groups, such as variants of the conjugacy search problem, the twisted conjugacy problem, the word problem, the multiple conjugacy problem, and analogues of the Diffie–Hellman and ElGamal problems formulated inside a (typically infinite) polycyclic group G chosen as a platform.

Quantum algorithms in the style of Shor and Kitaev efficiently solve the hidden subgroup problem (HSP) over finite abelian groups, and only partial results are known for finite non-abelian groups; no efficient quantum algorithm is currently known for HSP-type problems over infinite groups.

Problem. Determine whether public-key cryptosystems based on (infinite) polycyclic groups, with security reductions to standard search problems such as the conjugacy search problem, the twisted conjugacy problem, or the multiple conjugacy problem in a polycyclic platform group, are secure against polynomial-time quantum adversaries. More precisely: either exhibit a polynomial-time quantum algorithm that breaks one of these underlying search problems on a non-virtually-abelian infinite polycyclic group, or prove that no such algorithm exists (e.g., by establishing a quantum hardness result or a quantum lower bound for these problems on infinite polycyclic platforms).
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys, including the 2022 work "Group-based Cryptography in the Quantum Era" by Kahrobaei and Flores, continue to list quantum resistance of (infinite) polycyclic group-based cryptosystems as an open research direction; no polynomial-time quantum algorithm is currently known for HSP or conjugacy-type problems on infinite polycyclic groups, and no proof of quantum security has been established.

status_evidence.title: Group-based Cryptography in the Quantum Era
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys group-based cryptography with emphasis on quantum-era security; identifies non-abelian/infinite group platforms (including polycyclic) as candidates whose quantum resistance is not yet established.
status_evidence.claim: Quantum security of polycyclic group-based cryptosystems remains an open research direction.

status_evidence.title: Applications of Group Theory in Cryptography: Post-quantum Group-based Cryptography (AMS Surveys 278)
status_evidence.snippet: Monograph treating group-based cryptography as a post-quantum candidate area, with open problems on quantum cryptanalysis of polycyclic and related platforms.
status_evidence.claim: No known quantum algorithm breaks polycyclic-group-based schemes, but no proof of quantum security exists.
